source: Evans, Barston & Pollard (1983) On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning (Exp 1)
finding: Experiment 1: people accepted believable conclusions far more than unbelievable ones, and the belief effect was much larger on invalid arguments. This replaces the recalled numbers in b23.
numbers: N=24 undergraduates, 4 problems each. Percent accepting the conclusion: valid-believable 92, valid-unbelievable 46, invalid-believable 92, invalid-unbelievable 8. Correct 92% when logic agreed with belief, 27% when it conflicted. Belief effect p<.01, validity p<.02, interaction p<.05 (one-tailed sign tests).
limits: Tiny N and only 4 problems per person. Valid conclusions always had form C-A and invalid A-C, a figural confound the authors fixed in Exp 2. Acceptance rates, not signal-detection measures, so the interaction can be a response-bias artefact (see d04).
agent_relevance: Shows that stated-rule checking by humans is pulled by whether the conclusion is believable. A verify step (S8) should judge validity from the premises only and hide or ignore the believability of the conclusion.

source: Evans, Barston & Pollard (1983) Exp 2 and Exp 3
finding: Both later experiments replicated Exp 1 after removing the figure confound and after stressing logical necessity in the instructions. Belief bias stayed large; the belief-by-logic interaction stayed in the same direction.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=64, 4 groups of 16): valid-B 88, valid-U 56, invalid-B 72, invalid-U 13 (percent accepting). Correct 87% when logic agreed with belief, 48% when it conflicted. Belief p<.001, validity p<.001, interaction p<.01. Exp 3 (N=32, instructions stress logical necessity): valid-B 91, valid-U 53, invalid-B 67, invalid-U 6. Correct 97% vs 43%; interaction p=.067 one-tailed (not significant).
limits: Interaction fell just short in Exp 3. Same lab, same materials; no independent replication within the paper. Recalled figures in b23 (89/56/71/10) were close but not exact; use these.
agent_relevance: Stronger necessity wording did not remove the effect, so a prompt line like 'judge only from the premises' may reduce but not remove content bias in a model either. Test it on the model, not assume it.

source: Evans, Barston & Pollard (1983) verbal protocol analysis
finding: Verbal protocols showed two kinds of reasoners. When people accepted a valid-unbelievable conclusion they mentioned the premises more and irrelevant content less. When they rejected it, explanations looked like after-the-fact rationalisation of a belief-driven answer.
numbers: Exp 1 valid-unbelievable: interaction of response with mentions of irrelevant information p=.026 (one-tailed Fisher). Exp 2 (pooled groups): response by premise mentions chi2=24.61, p<.001; by irrelevant mentions chi2=15.11, p<.001. Retrospective, concurrent and no-verbalisation groups showed the same trends.
limits: Protocols are self-report and may not reflect the true process; authors themselves offer both readings (rationalisation vs real premise-to-conclusion reasoning).
agent_relevance: Explanations given after an answer can be rationalisations. A model's written justification after its verdict is weak evidence the verdict came from the premises; check the derivation, not the story.

source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang & Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical-Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data (Psychon Bull Rev; OSF preprint read)
finding: Re-analysis of 22 confidence-rating studies found ROC curves are not systematically asymmetric and, on average, believability does not change how well people discriminate valid from invalid syllogisms. This supports the response-bias account of Dube, Rotello and Heit (2010) at group level, but individual differences (for example analytic style) moderate it.
numbers: 22 studies, N=993. Group-level ROC slope estimates were very close to 1 with credible intervals spanning above and below 1. Believable and unbelievable discriminability posteriors almost fully overlapped. New forced-choice test: effect of choice focus -0.03 [-0.08, 0.02], Bayes factor 69.72 for ROC symmetry. Equal-variance SDT fits fail at ceiling (their Study 2).
limits: Authors say it is a new starting point, not a final word. Aggregate null can hide opposite effects in subgroups (mental-model reasoners vs transitive-chain reasoners). Dube et al. 2010 itself was not opened; its claims are taken from this paper's description. Heit and Rotello 2014 not opened.
agent_relevance: K22 should read: the accuracy cost of unbelievable conclusions looks mostly like a shift in how willing people are to say valid, not worse reasoning, on average. For the agent: track false-accept and false-reject rates separately in verify checks, because a content-driven shift in the threshold can look like an accuracy change.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' logical reasoning via automated puzzle generation from SAT formulas
finding: Closest benchmark to the stated-rules-contradict question. 2,100 natural-language puzzles from CNF formulas, each asking whether all conditions can hold together. Models are much worse on UNSAT than SAT when instances are hard; most models are near coin-flip on hard UNSAT.
numbers: Zero-shot, 50% random baseline. Overall: o4-mini 89.3, DeepSeek-R1 87.8, DeepSeek-V3 84.0, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 74.8, GPT-4o 58.0, gpt-4o-mini 53.9, Llama3.1-8B 38.2. Hard (31-50 clauses) UNSAT: o4-mini 65.0, R1 83.6, DeepSeek-V3 74.3, Claude-3.7 42.1, GPT-4o 18.9, gpt-4o-mini 13.2. Average over 20 models on hard: SAT 66.7, UNSAT 39.3, overall 53.0. Easy UNSAT: o4-mini 98.2, R1 98.2.
limits: Paper abstract says hard UNSAT is near random for the strongest model (o4-mini 65.0) but R1 reached 83.6 on hard UNSAT in Table 3, so the headline is model-dependent. Low UNSAT accuracy in small models means they say SAT by default. Puzzles have 36 variables and 55 sentences on average, larger than typical agent rule sets.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 answer: frontier reasoning models can detect an inconsistent natural-language rule set well when the set is small (about 98% on easy UNSAT) and degrade with size. Weaker models mostly say satisfiable. Treat a no-contradiction verdict from a small model as weak, and prefer a solver for large rule sets.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench error and trace analysis
finding: Right label is not enough. When models say SAT they often give no valid assignment (satisfiability bias). Judged reasoning traces are valid less often than labels are correct.
numbers: Table 4 (prediction accuracy vs trace-valid): o4-mini SAT 94.7 vs 74.6, UNSAT 83.6 vs 74.1; DeepSeek-R1 SAT 85.2 vs 73.8, UNSAT 90.3 vs 82.1; DeepSeek-V3 SAT 82.9 vs 65.7; Claude-3.7 SAT 83.2 vs 47.4. Error types (Table 5), o4-mini / R1: satisfiability bias 68.7 / 40.5%, context inconsistency 17.0 / 44.7%, condition omission 14.3 / 12.6%, spurious priors 0.0 / 2.1%. GPT-4o accuracy fell to about 50% near 30 clauses.
limits: Trace validity judged by GPT-4o (human check of 100 puzzles: judge correct 93%). Error classes were assigned by GPT-4o too, so counts are approximate.
agent_relevance: When the agent asserts these rules are consistent, require a concrete assignment that is checked clause by clause. Condition omission and self-contradiction in the trace are the main failure classes to guard.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench: natural-language framing, translation checks and error-aware prompts
finding: Wrapping the same formula in a story makes it harder. Their own dataset pipeline used back-translation (NL to formula, then solver equivalence check) and found a small but real translation-error rate. Adding failure-mode reminders to the prompt fixed many errors.
numbers: Table 6 (puzzle vs raw formula): gpt-4o-mini 53.6 vs 54.8, GPT-4o 58.2 vs 59.2, DeepSeek-V3 84.0 vs 87.3, o4-mini 89.4 vs 94.3. Human check of 100 puzzles: clause translation faithful in 97 (3 minor errors, e.g. a conditional rendered with the wrong if-then), mapping errors 0. Error-aware prompt corrected 60.4% of previously failed cases for o4-mini and 73.2% for DeepSeek-R1. LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-14B on 1,100 traces: 51.9 to 53.6.
limits: Prompt-fix numbers apply to cases that had already failed (selection effect); no equal-token control and no measure of new errors introduced. Number of puzzles discarded by the equivalence check is not reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: an NL-to-formula back-check by a solver caught translation drift in the dataset build, and residual error was about 3% on a 100-item human sample. Errors cluster on conditionals and negation. A failure-pattern reminder in the verify prompt is cheap, but its gain is unmeasured on fresh items.

source: Zhao et al. (2025/2026) SATQuest: verifier for logical reasoning evaluation and reinforcement fine-tuning
finding: SAT-based tasks including finding a minimal unsatisfiable subset (the contradicting rules). Diagnostic tasks (MCS, MUS) were the hardest class for all models, and top models fabricate solver calls or shortcuts as instances grow.
numbers: Overall accuracy across 5 task types x 4 formats: o3-mini 0.56, DeepSeek-R1 0.42, QwQ-32B 0.40, GPT-4.1 0.38, DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.36, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 0.08. Task difficulty order: decision and search highest, then MaxSAT, MCS and MUS lowest. o3-mini response length falls at high complexity on MUS and MCS (abandons reasoning for invented shortcuts).
limits: Per-cell MUS accuracies were not extractable from the figure text; only ordering and overall scores are recorded. Instances are random CNF (clauses = 4 x variables, up to 16 variables), not realistic rule sets. Version 2 dated July 2026.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partial: identifying which rules clash is much harder than saying that some clash. For S8, a model asked which rules conflict needs an external check (even a simple pairwise or subset test) rather than a free-form answer.

source: Feng et al. (2025) VeriCoT: neuro-symbolic chain-of-thought validation via logical consistency checks, Table 1
finding: Solver-checked CoT verification (SMT, Claude-3.5-Sonnet-V2) is precise but covers a minority of chains. Most chains fail as ungrounded (unstated premises) rather than contradictory.
numbers: Verified chains (pass rate / precision / task accuracy): ProofWriter 45.2 / 94.1 / 75.8; BioASQ 25.3 / 84.3 / 81.4; LegalBench-SARA 15.2 / 87.0 / 80.0. Baselines: Explanation-Refiner pass 14.8, 1.5, 6.8; direct SMT baseline pass 10.0, 5.9, 4.8. Without explicit premise generation pass rate drops to 3.3, 2.9, 0.6.
limits: Real SMT solver, not prompt-only. One executor model. Precision beats task accuracy by 18.3 points on ProofWriter but only 2.9 on BioASQ and 7.0 on SARA. Single group.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partial: an abstain-if-unverifiable rule gives a strong signal where rules are formal (ProofWriter) but would discard 55% to 85% of chains here. Coverage cost is large; do not gate answers on verification alone.

source: Feng et al. (2025) VeriCoT Table 3: using the verifier signal for self-reflection
finding: Feeding solver failure reasons back to the model raised pass rates a lot but task accuracy barely moved, and fell on ProofWriter. Translation (untranslatable) errors did not shrink after reflection.
numbers: After reflection, VeriCoT-Base pass / precision / VCAR / task accuracy: ProofWriter 60.1 (+14.9) / 90.1 (-4.0) / 54.1 / 74.1 (was 75.8); BioASQ 33.4 (+8.1) / 86.3 / 28.8 / 82.0 (was 81.4); SARA 25.2 (+10.0) / 85.5 / 21.6 / 81.4 (was 80.0). With LLM-judge premise feedback: pass 60.6, 36.9, 23.0; accuracy 73.7, 80.5, 81.0.
limits: Pre-reflection task accuracy taken from Table 1. The paper text claims consistent gains; the table shows -1.7 on ProofWriter. Single model, one run.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 8: repair guided by a checker makes chains verifiable more often than it makes them right. Same lesson as Logic-LM++ (d11): optimise accuracy, not pass rate.

source: Kirtania, Gupta & Radhakrishna (2024) Logic-LM++: multi-step refinement for symbolic formulations (Table 1, RQ2)
finding: Plain refinement of a formal translation can keep it executable while changing its meaning. Adding a pairwise check of which version matches the English better, with revert-if-not-better, helped GPT-4 but not GPT-3.5. This is a semantic back-check against the task text.
numbers: FOLIO (204 test items) accuracy: GPT-3.5 Standard 45.09, CoT 57.35, Logic-LM 62.80, Logic-LM++ 62.25; GPT-4 Standard 69.11, CoT 70.58, Logic-LM 78.92, Logic-LM++ 84.80. ProofWriter GPT-4 79.66 both; AR-LSAT GPT-4 43.04 to 46.32. Backtracking agent raised execution accuracy about 6% (GPT-4) and 3% (GPT-3.5).
limits: Judge and generator are the same LLM family; single run; no token accounting for the extra comparison calls. GPT-3.5 result is -0.55, within noise.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: a compare-with-the-original check helps a strong model (+5.9 on FOLIO) and is neutral for a weak one. It is a form of back-translation check; its cost is one extra call per revision.

source: Lalwani et al. (2025) Autoformalizing natural language to first-order logic: a case study in logical fallacy detection (NL2FOL), Table 2
finding: Pipeline: LLM translates to FOL, an SMT solver (CVC4) checks whether the negation is satisfiable (a counter-model means invalid). It beat direct judgement on real-world text but lost on the clean in-distribution set where strong models already do well.
numbers: F1, LOGIC / LogicClimate: GPT-4o end-to-end 0.96 / 0.58 vs NL2FOL 0.78 / 0.80; GPT-4o-mini end-to-end 0.91 / 0.60 vs NL2FOL 0.75 / 0.77; Llama-7B end-to-end 0.58 / 0.47 vs NL2FOL 0.71 / 0.73; o1-preview end-to-end 0.93 / 0.67 and NL2FOL failed to complete in most cases. NL2FOL has high recall (0.82 to 0.94), end-to-end has high precision.
limits: Authors note end-to-end models may have seen the LOGIC dataset in training (web-sourced). Fallacy detection, not rule-set consistency; SNLI sentences used as valid negatives.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 and gap 1: counter-model search wins where direct judging is unreliable (out-of-distribution text, small models) and loses to a strong reasoning model on familiar items. The reasoning model's failure to follow the multi-stage format is itself a cost.

source: Lalwani et al. (2025) NL2FOL ablations: SMT solver vs LLM, grounding, error sources (Tables 4-6)
finding: Holding the translated logical form fixed, the SMT counter-model check beat GPT-4o judging the same formula. Most pipeline errors came from missing or wrong background knowledge, not from the formula writer.
numbers: SMT vs GPT-4o as classifier on the same forms (LOGIC F1 / LogicClimate F1): 0.78 / 0.80 vs 0.66 / 0.73. Accuracy 0.78 vs 0.69 and 0.80 vs 0.73. Grounding (GPT-4o-mini, LOGIC F1): no grounding 0.66, LLM without context 0.75, LLM with context 0.78, BART-MNLI 0.70. Error source in 100 manually reviewed failures: background-knowledge retriever 54%, property extractor 13%, FOL formulation 13%, remainder in claim and implication identification.
limits: Counter-model search was compared with an LLM judge on the formula, not with proof search; no direct counter-model vs proof-search test exists in these sources. Domain experts labeled errors on 100 items.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partial: bounded counter-model construction (satisfy premises and negated conclusion) is the right form of check for invalidity and works better than asking an LLM to judge. Whether it beats proof search was not tested. The weak point is missing implicit premises, so list assumed background facts explicitly before checking.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Faithful logical reasoning via symbolic chain-of-thought (SymbCoT): verifier and cost
finding: A prompt-only verifier (no external solver) re-checks the translation and each deduction. It removed the remaining unfaithful correct answers in a small manual check, but costs about a third of all output tokens.
numbers: Manual faithfulness check on FOLIO (five graduate annotators, majority vote): CoT 6% correct-by-flawed-reasoning, SymbCoT without verifier 2%, with verifier 0%. Ablation (GPT-4): planner plus solver removal -10.4 points on average, translator removal -6.3. Average output tokens per module (ProntoQA / ProofWriter / FOLIO / LogicalDeduction / AR-LSAT): translator 324/290/145/176/323, planner 198/202/313/251/627, solver 214/216/330/282/654, verifier 384/353/334/472/726. Execution rate 100% vs Logic-LM 17.7 points lower on average. GPT-3.5 FOLIO did not beat Logic-LM.
limits: Verifier-only ablation accuracy is plotted in a figure and was not recoverable from the text. Faithfulness sample is small (N not stated). GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023) only. Verifier share of output tokens by my sums: FOLIO 334 of 1,122 (30%), ProofWriter 353 of 1,061 (33%).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a prompt-only verifier is feasible and buys faithfulness, but it adds roughly 30% tokens, which an equal-token test must charge to it. No abstain or coverage numbers are reported; the claimed gain is on answers, not on selective answering.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Logic-of-Thought: injecting logic into contexts (contraposition ablation)
finding: Extracting propositions, expanding them with propositional laws (including contraposition) and adding the results to the prompt helped weaker models more than GPT-4. Removing the contraposition step cost about 3.8 points on a 135-item FOLIO subset.
numbers: FOLIO closed-world subset (N=135): GPT-3.5 Direct 68.89, LoT 76.00; GPT-4 Direct 82.96, LoT 83.55 (+0.59). With CoT: GPT-4 85.33 to 85.48. Ablation Table 4: LoT 76.00, without Contraposition Law 72.22, with only half the generated logic text 72.96. Their re-run of LINC on this subset: GPT-3.5 45.19, GPT-4 55.56 (far below LINC's own 72.5). Datasets and N: ReClor 46, ProofWriter depth-5 985, RuleTaker depth-5 967, LogiQA 1,302.
limits: Table 4 says GPT-4 but the 76.00 baseline matches the GPT-3.5 cell, so the model in the ablation is unclear. A 3.8-point change on 135 items is about 5 items, within noise. Contraposition was never tested alone, only removed from a bundle. Not a modus tollens-specific test; no reasoning model tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: explicit contrapositive expansion may help a 2023 weak model slightly and does nothing for GPT-4 (+0.6). No evidence yet for reasoning models. Low priority as a standalone step.

source: Chen, Zhang & Tao (2025) JustLogic: a benchmark for deductive reasoning in LLMs (reasoning-model results, argument forms)
finding: Reasoning models do beat older ones, but unevenly. DeepSeek-R1 exceeded the human average; o1 was below it because it answered Uncertain prematurely at high depth. Across models, modus tollens, disjunctive syllogism and reductio were harder than hypothetical syllogism and constructive dilemma.
numbers: Accuracy: human average 73.0, DeepSeek-R1 80.9, o1 72.9, GPT-4o 65.6, o1-mini 62.0, R1-Distill-Qwen-14B 61.7, Llama3-70B 53.1, Llama3-8B 49.8. o1 answered Uncertain for 90% of depth-7 questions. Extended table: GPT-4o on JustLogic easy/medium/hard/very hard 77.3/63.3/57.3/53.0, LogiQA2.0 64.5, FOLIO 76.3; DeepSeek-R1 90.0/83.3/68.0/65.0, LogiQA2.0 87.6, FOLIO 86.2.
limits: R1 FOLIO figure (86.2) comes from a side table with unspecified subset and N. Per-model modus tollens numbers are in a figure only. o1 test-compute may have been limited by the API (authors' own guess).
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and gap 6: R1 chain-of-thought alone scores 86.2 on FOLIO, above the 2023 GPT-4 solver pipelines (Logic-LM 78.92, d11) without any solver. Modus tollens stays a relatively weak form even for reasoning models.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: scaling limits of LLMs for logical reasoning (Table 1)
finding: On constraint-satisfaction logic grid puzzles, reasoning models are far ahead of non-reasoning models, but all fall off sharply as the search space grows (the curse of complexity).
numbers: Overall puzzle accuracy: o1-full 81.0, DeepSeek-R1 78.7, o1-preview 71.4, o1-mini 59.7, Claude Sonnet 3.5 36.2, Llama-3.1-405B 32.6, GPT-4o 31.7. X-Large puzzles (search space above 10^9): o1-full 42.5, R1 28.5, o1-preview 17.0, o1-mini 12.0, non-reasoning models 0 to 1.0. Hidden reasoning tokens averaged about 5,145 (o1-mini) and 5,346 (o1-preview) vs 503 and 544 for GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o; about 400 hidden tokens per Z3 conflict below 20 conflicts, then a plateau.
limits: Column labels in the extracted table are ambiguous; the X-Large and overall figures were cross-checked against the text (o1-preview 17.0 on X-Large). Puzzles are search problems with a unique solution, not consistency checks. Not measured against a solver at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: on search-heavy tasks, reasoning models spend about 10x tokens and still collapse at large size, which is where an exact solver would help most. On small deduction tasks they already match solver pipelines.

source: Lin et al. (2025) ZebraLogic: best-of-N, majority voting and self-verification on GPT-4o
finding: Many samples contain a correct answer, but majority vote and reward models cannot find it. Only an oracle selector gets the gain. This is the quantitative reason an external checker could be valuable.
numbers: GPT-4o baseline 31.7 overall. Majority vote N=32: 38.0 (N=128: 37.6). Best-of-N with oracle selection: N=32 60.3, N=128 69.1. Reward-model selection N=32: 34.8 (worse than majority vote). Self-verify prompting: gains of about 1 point or less in the table rows that could be read.
limits: Table layout partly garbled in extraction; GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini only, not reasoning models. Oracle bound, not a method. Disagreement among samples was not used to trigger anything.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partial: the gap between oracle (60 to 69) and vote (38) is large, so a verifier has headroom. No source tested calling the solver only when samples disagree. That test is still open.

source: Chen, Zhou & Zhang (2026) PRoSFI: process reward over structured formal intermediates, ProverQA Hard and Extra
finding: An R1-Zero-style outcome-reward RL run on a 7B model reaches over 90% on ProverQA Hard, but only about 22% of its reasoning chains are sound. Checking steps with a formal prover raises soundness to 76% at equal answer accuracy.
numbers: ProverQA Hard / Extra (16 samples averaged, Extra N=128): outcome-reward CoT answer correct 91.31 / 86.96, GPT-judged soundness 21.97 / 11.87; direct Lean generation answer 92.29 / 83.15, soundness 33.11 / 10.45; PRoSFI answer 92.97 / 91.94, soundness 76.07 / 56.10. Direct Lean compile hit rate 13.77% (Hard), 4.35% (Extra). Majority voting over more samples did not raise soundness for outcome-CoT. For scale, GPT-4o CoT scores 50.0 on ProverQA Hard in the original paper (Qi et al. 2025, opened).
limits: Trained on the ProverQA distribution; soundness judged by GPT, not a prover. Single model size. Training result, not a prompt-only scaffold.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: on ProverQA Hard, answer accuracy alone no longer separates methods once a model is trained on it; answer-correct but unsound chains are the real issue. A step-level formal check is where a solver still adds something. Not a prompt-only result.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats confuse reasoning LLM: query-agnostic adversarial triggers for reasoning models (COLM 2025)
finding: Irrelevant appended text (for example the cat-sleep fact) raises error rates of reasoning models on math problems and lengthens their output. Distractor sensitivity persists in R1, o1 and o3-mini class models. Math only, not logic or premise order.
numbers: 225 math problems, three triggers. DeepSeek-R1 combined attack success 4.50% vs 1.50% random error (3x); R1-distill-Qwen-32B 8.00% (2.83x). Transfer on 1,000 GSM8K items: reasoning-model combined factors up to 5.2x; instruction-tuned up to 7.2x. Responses at least 1.5x longer: o1 26.4%, o3-mini 16.8%, R1 28.0%, R1-distill-32B 42.2%.
limits: Headline 300% increase is relative; absolute rise for R1 is 3 percentage points. Triggers were searched adversarially against a proxy model. Tests math, not logic; no premise-order variant.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: distractors still hurt reasoning models, and they cost tokens. No source tests premise order in reasoning models or a restate-in-dependency-order step. Premise-order result in 2025-2026 models stays unmeasured.

source: Kalyanpur et al. (2024) LLM-ARC: enhancing LLMs with an automated reasoning critic (FOLIO)
finding: An LLM writes logic-program code plus unit tests for semantic correctness; an ASP solver runs them and returns failures for up to 4 retries. Test generation was the main gain over code-only.
numbers: FOLIO accuracy: GPT-4-turbo zero-shot about 67, CoT about 74, best LLM-only (GPT-4 fine-tuned on 1K examples) 80.7, Logic-LM 78.9, LLM-ARC-8-shot (no tests) 74.62, 8-shot with tests 81.22 (+6.6), 20-shot 83.25, 20-shot with tests 85.79, trained actor on 918 critic dialog traces 88.32. Retries add 4 to 5 points and plateau after two. Using FOL as an intermediate step in CoT did not help.
limits: Row-to-number mapping read from a garbled table and checked against the text (+6.6 test-gen gain, 88.32 best). GPT-4 era; no reasoning model; no equal-token comparison; tests are written by the same LLM that wrote the code.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: LLM-written semantic tests (assert what the English says must follow) act as a back-translation check and added 6.6 points for the 8-shot variant. The same tests could be added to a prompt-only verify step.

source: Xie et al. (2025) Logic-RL: rule-based RL on Knights and Knaves (Table 2: reasoning models on K&K)
finding: Strong reasoning models vary hugely on a small puzzle family that a truth-table search solves exactly. o3-mini-high is almost perfect; o1 drops off quickly with more people; R1 is flat but lower.
numbers: Average accuracy over 2 to 8 people: o3-mini-high 0.94, DeepSeek-R1 0.81, o1-2024-12-17 0.42, GPT-4o 0.37, GPT-4o-mini 0.25, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M 0.19; Logic-RL 7B 0.89 after RL on under 5,000 synthetic 3 to 7 person puzzles (8-person OOD 0.67). o3-mini-high on 8 people 0.83, o1 0.20.
limits: Synthetic puzzles with one logic type; single run per cell. No solver baseline reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: reasoning-model performance is model-specific, so a claim that reasoning models already match a solver cannot be generalised from one model. Choose the checking step per model and measure it.
